q: Which emperor was stabbed to death in the street?
reply:
**Conclusion:** **Cao Mao (Cao Mao)**, emperor of Wei, often called **Gaoguixiang Gong** after his death. He was stabbed to death in **260 CE** by **Cheng Ji**, acting under the orders of **Jia Chong**, a key man in **Sima Zhao**’s faction.

**Evidence:** In the *Sanguozhi* (*Wei Shu*, annals of Cao Mao), Cao Mao is described as resenting Sima Zhao’s control and leading guards and servants out to attack him. Pei Songzhi’s commentary, quoting *Han Jin Chun Qiu*, says that at the **south gate tower (Nan Que)**, Jia Chong’s men blocked Cao Mao. When Cao Mao fought personally, Cheng Ji asked Jia Chong what to do; Jia Chong told him to act. Cheng Ji then stabbed Cao Mao, and the blade came out his back. He died there. Sima Zhao later used Cheng Ji as a scapegoat and had him killed.

So the precise record says he was killed at the **south gate tower / under the gate**, not literally “in the street.” The *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* uses the same event, with some dramatic coloring.

q: Who were the sons of Emperor Zhaolie?
reply:
**Conclusion:** According to the *Sanguozhi*, Emperor Zhaolie — Liu Bei — had **three recorded biological sons**: **Liu Shan** (刘禅), **Liu Yong** (刘永), and **Liu Li** (刘理). He also had an **adopted son**, **Liu Feng** (刘封), who was not a biological son.

**Evidence from the *Sanguozhi*:**
- **Liu Shan**: In the *Shu Shu*, *Houzhu Zhuan*, he is recorded as “后主讳禅，字公嗣，先主子也” — “The Later Ruler was named Shan, courtesy name Gongsi, a son of the Former Lord [Liu Bei].” He became Liu Bei’s heir and succeeded him.
- **Liu Yong**: In the *Shu Shu*, *Liu Yong Zhuan*, he is recorded as “刘永字公寿，先主子，后主庶弟也” — “Liu Yong, courtesy name Gongshou, a son of the Former Lord and a younger half-brother of the Later Ruler.” He was enfeoffed as Lu Wang and later Ganling Wang.
- **Liu Li**: In the *Shu Shu*, *Liu Li Zhuan*, he is recorded as “刘理字奉孝，亦后主庶弟也，与永异母” — “Liu Li, courtesy name Fengxiao, also a younger half-brother of the Later Ruler, and by a different mother from Liu Yong.” He was enfeoffed as Liang Wang and later Anping Wang.
- **Liu Feng**: In the *Shu Shu*, *Liu Feng Zhuan*, he is recorded as “刘封者，本罗侯寇氏之子，长沙刘氏之甥也。先主至荆州，以未有继嗣，养封为子” — “Liu Feng was originally a son of the Kou family of Luohou and a nephew of the Liu family of Changsha. When the Former Lord came to Jingzhou, because he had no heir yet, he adopted Liu Feng as his son.” He was later ordered to die by Liu Bei.

**Romance vs. history:** The *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* follows the same basic list. It does not add other sons; the main differences are literary emphasis, not the recorded set of Liu Bei’s sons.

q: How many emperors did the state of Wu have?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The state of Wu (Eastern Wu) had **four emperors who actually reigned as emperors**: Sun Quan, Sun Liang, Sun Xiu, and Sun Hao.

**List of reigning Wu emperors:**

1. **Sun Quan** (孙权) — Emperor Da / Great Emperor; reigned as emperor **229–252**.
2. **Sun Liang** (孙亮) — reigned **252–258**; deposed.
3. **Sun Xiu** (孙休) — Emperor Jing; reigned **258–264**.
4. **Sun Hao** (孙皓) — reigned **264–280**; surrendered to Jin in 280, ending Wu.

**Evidence from the *Sanguozhi*:**  
Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi* places Sun Quan in the *Wu Shu*, “Biography of the Lord of Wu” (卷47), and then treats Sun Liang, Sun Xiu, and Sun Hao together in the “Biography of the Three Successor Lords” (卷48). Pei Songzhi’s commentary fills in details but does not change this basic succession.

**Important distinction:**  
If one counts **posthumously honored emperors**, the number changes: Sun Jian (孙权’s father) was posthumously honored as Emperor Wulie, and Sun He (Sun Hao’s father) was later posthumously honored as Emperor Wen. But neither actually reigned as emperor of Wu. Sun Ce was posthumously honored only as Prince Huan of Changsha, not as emperor.

So, for the practical historical question “how many emperors did Wu have?” the answer is **four**.

q: How many different people named Ma Zhong appear in the Records of the Three Kingdoms?
reply:
**Two distinct people named Ma Zhong (马忠) appear in Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi*.**

1. **Ma Zhong of Shu Han**  
   - Courtesy name **Dexin (德信)**.  
   - He has a biography in *Sanguozhi*, Shu 13.  
   - He was from Baxi Langzhong, served Liu Bei and later Zhuge Liang, and was active in the southern campaigns.

2. **Ma Zhong of Wu**  
   - He was a **sima** under Wu general **Pan Zhang (潘璋)**.  
   - He is recorded as the one who captured **Guan Yu (关羽)**, Guan Ping, and Zhao Lei at Linju/Zhangxiang.  
   - This appears in *Sanguozhi*, Wu 10 (Pan Zhang’s biography) and also in Wu 9 (Lü Meng’s biography).

These two are different men. In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, the Wu Ma Zhong is given a larger role and is sometimes confused with the Shu Ma Zhong, but in the *Sanguozhi* they are two separate figures. As far as Chen Shou’s main text goes, the count is **two**; I am not aware of a third distinct Ma Zhong in Pei Songzhi’s annotations either.

q: Who were Xun Yu's sons, and what offices did each of them hold?
reply:
**Conclusion (based on *Sanguozhi* and Pei Songzhi’s commentary):**  
The sons of Xun Yu 荀彧 recorded there are chiefly five:

| Son | Courtesy name | Office recorded |
|---|---|---|
| Xun Yun 荀恽 | Changqian 长倩 | Huben Zhonglangjiang 虎贲中郎将 |
| Xun Yu 荀俣 (Yǔ) | Shuqian 叔倩 | Yushi Zhongcheng 御史中丞 |
| Xun Shen 荀诜 | Manqian 曼倩 | Military Advisor to the General-in-Chief (Dajiangjun Junshi 大将军军师) |
| Xun Yi 荀顗 | Jingqian 景倩 | Sikong 司空 |
| Xun Can 荀粲 | Fengqian 奉倩 | Sanqi Changshi 散骑常侍 |

**Evidence and notes:**  
- The main text of the *Sanguozhi* (*Wei Shu* 10, “Xun Yu zhuan”) says Xun Yu’s son **Xun Yun 荀恽** inherited his title; it gives Xun Yun’s office as **Huben Zhonglangjiang 虎贲中郎将**.  
- Pei Songzhi’s commentary, quoting the *Xun family traditions* (*Xunshi Jiazhuan* 荀氏家传), adds the other sons and their offices: **Xun Yu 荀俣** as **Yushi Zhongcheng 御史中丞**, **Xun Shen 荀诜** as **Dajiangjun Junshi 大将军军师**, **Xun Yi 荀顗** as **Sikong 司空**, and **Xun Can 荀粲** as **Sanqi Changshi 散骑常侍**.  
- For **Xun Yi 荀顗**, other sources such as the *Jin Shu* add that he later became **Taiwei 太尉** and was enfeoffed as **Duke of Linhuai 临淮公**, but the *Sanguozhi*/Pei note itself records him as reaching **Sikong 司空**.  
- I cannot confirm from the *Sanguozhi*/Pei note any further sons of Xun Yu beyond these recorded ones.

q: Why did Cao Cao flee from Luoyang?
reply:
In the official histories, **Cao Cao did not flee Luoyang because of a failed assassination attempt on Dong Zhuo**. He left/fled east because Dong Zhuo had seized control of the court, appointed Cao Cao as **Xiaoqi Xiaowei**, and wanted to use him; Cao Cao refused to serve Dong Zhuo, changed his name, and slipped away east. He went to **Chenliu**, raised troops, and prepared to attack Dong Zhuo.

**Evidence from *Sanguozhi* (Wudi Ji):**  
After Dong Zhuo entered Luoyang, deposed Emperor Shao, and installed Emperor Xian:

> “卓表太祖为骁骑校尉，欲与计事。太祖乃变易姓名，间行东归……太祖至陈留，散家财，合义兵，将以诛卓。”

That is: Dong Zhuo memorialized Cao Cao as Xiaoqi Xiaowei and wanted to consult/use him. Cao Cao then changed his name and traveled secretly east. When he reached Chenliu, he dispersed his family wealth, gathered “righteous troops,” and planned to punish Dong Zhuo.

**Pei Songzhi’s notes** add the famous Zhongmu episode: on the way out, Cao Cao was suspected by a village headman at Zhongmu and detained, but someone recognized him and helped get him released. This is the historical context, not an assassination plot.

**The *Sanguo Yanyi* version:**  
In the novel, Cao Cao borrows Wang Yun’s “Seven-Star Sword,” tries to assassinate Dong Zhuo, fails, pretends he was presenting the sword, and then flees Luoyang. That is **Romance fiction**; it is not in the *Sanguozhi* main text or Pei’s notes.

q: When Zhuge Liang lit the seven-star lamps at Wuzhang Plains to prolong his life, who burst in and put them out?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, the person who burst in and accidentally extinguished the lamp was **Wei Yan (魏延, Wèi Yán)**. He did not do it deliberately: he rushed in to report an urgent military situation, and in his haste he knocked over or put out the **main lamp (主灯)** of Zhuge Liang’s seven-star lamp ritual.

**Basis:** In the *Romance* episode at Wuzhang Plains, Zhuge Liang (诸葛亮, Zhūgě Liàng) tries to prolong his life by lighting seven-star lamps; if the main lamp stays lit for seven days, he can gain more years. On the critical night, Wei Yan bursts in with news of Sima Yi’s (司马懿, Sīmǎ Yì) forces, and the main lamp is extinguished. Zhuge Liang then sighs that life and death are fated.

**Historical note:** This is **not** in Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi* or Pei Songzhi’s annotations. Official history only records that Zhuge Liang fell ill and died at Wuzhang Plains in 234, during the stalemate with Sima Yi. There is no seven-star lamp ritual or Wei Yan extinguishing a lamp in the official histories. So the scene is a *Romance* invention.

q: How did Chang Ho die?
reply:
Zhang He (Chang Ho) died in 231 CE from an arrow wound suffered at Mumen (木门) while pursuing Zhuge Liang’s retreating army.

**Official history (Sanguozhi main text):**  
In the *Sanguozhi*, Zhang He’s biography says: after Zhuge Liang withdrew, Zhang He pursued to Mumen and fought Zhuge Liang’s army. A “flying arrow” hit Zhang He in the right knee, and he died. He was given the posthumous title Marquis Zhuang (壮侯).

**Pei Songzhi’s annotation:**  
Pei Songzhi quotes the *Weilue*, which adds that Sima Yi ordered Zhang He to pursue. Zhang He objected, saying, “A returning army should not be pursued” (*归军勿追*). Sima Yi did not listen, so Zhang He had to advance. The Shu army then set an ambush from high ground and fired many crossbow bolts/arrows; Zhang He was hit in the thigh (*髀*).

So the official record is slightly inconsistent on the exact wound: the main text says **right knee**, while the *Weilue* note says **thigh**. But both agree he died from an arrow wound at Mumen.

**Romance vs. history:**  
In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, Zhang He’s death is dramatized as an ambush at Mumen, where he is killed by a volley of arrows. The official history has the same core event—death by arrow at Mumen while pursuing Zhuge Liang—but is less dramatic and does not describe a “thousand arrows” scene.

q: At Hefei, facing Sun Quan's army of a hundred thousand, how many picked men did Zhang Liao lead in his charge?
reply:
Zhang Liao led **800 picked men** in that charge.

According to the *Sanguozhi* (Chen Shou), in Zhang Liao’s biography: when Sun Quan came to Hefei with a claimed 100,000 troops, Zhang Liao “night-recruited brave men willing to follow him, and obtained 800 men.” The next morning he armored up, took a halberd, charged the enemy line, killed dozens, killed two generals, and fought his way to Sun Quan’s command standard. He then broke out and went back to rescue the rest of his 800.

So the figure is **800**. This is also the figure used in the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*; it is not a Romance-only invention. The main source is *Sanguozhi*, Wei Shu 17, *Zhang Liao zhuan*.

q: During his southern campaign, how many times did Zhuge Liang capture and release Meng Huo?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In the *Sanguozhi* tradition, the figure is **seven times**—Zhuge Liang captured and released Meng Huo in **seven** cycles. But this comes from **Pei Songzhi’s commentary**, not from Chen Shou’s main text.

**Evidence:**
- Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi* main biography of Zhuge Liang only says: “In the spring of the third year, Liang led the army on a southern campaign; by autumn all was pacified.” It does **not** mention Meng Huo or any number of captures/releases.
- Pei Songzhi’s annotation quotes the *Han Jin Chun Qiu*: after Meng Huo was captured and shown the camps, he said he could win if released. Zhuge Liang laughed and released him to fight again. The text says: **“七纵七禽”**—“released him seven times and captured him seven times.” After the seventh, Meng Huo finally submitted and said the southerners would not rebel again.

So: **seven times** according to Pei Songzhi’s cited source; the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* popularized this as the famous “seven captures and seven releases.” Chen Shou’s main text alone does not give the number.

q: Where did Taishi Ci and Sun Ce fight each other? Later, when Taishi Ci was captured, how did Sun Ce treat him?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The famous duel between Taishi Ci and Sun Ce took place at **Shenting** (Shenting; in the novel, “Shenting Ridge”). Taishi Ci was not captured there. Later he was captured at **Jingxian**. Sun Ce treated him generously: he personally untied him, took his hand, reminded him of Shenting, and offered to share his enterprise with him. He appointed Taishi Ci as **Menxia Du** and later gave him troops and the title **Zhechong Zhonglangjiang**.

**Evidence from the historical record:**  
In the *Sanguozhi* (Wu Shu, Taishi Ci zhuan), the duel is placed at Shenting: Sun Ce and Taishi Ci fought there; Sun Ce stabbed Taishi Ci’s horse and seized his hand-halberd, while Taishi Ci seized Sun Ce’s helmet. Reinforcements then arrived on both sides, and the fight broke off.

Later, after Liu Yao’s defeat, Taishi Ci was captured at Jingxian. Sun Ce “untied him and took his hand,” asking: “Do you still remember Shenting? If you had captured me then, what would you have done?” Taishi Ci replied, “It is hard to say.” Sun Ce laughed and said, “Today’s business, I will share with you.” He then made Taishi Ci **Menxia Du**; later he returned to Wu, gave him troops, and appointed him **Zhechong Zhonglangjiang**. He also trusted Taishi Ci to go to Yuzhang to pacify Liu Yao’s remaining followers, and Taishi Ci returned as promised.

**Romance vs. history:**  
The *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* dramatizes the duel at **Shenting Ridge** and adds details such as Sun Ce giving Taishi Ci his own clothes. But the core points—the fight at Shenting, the later capture at Jingxian, and Sun Ce’s generous treatment—are based on the historical *Sanguozhi* record, not invented by the novel.

q: How did Cao Cao view Liu Bei when Liu Bei came over to his side?
reply:
**Conclusion:** Cao Cao did **not** see Liu Bei as an ordinary refugee or subordinate. He saw him as an outstanding “hero” (*yingxiong*) and a potential rival—someone worth honoring, using, and also watching closely. He treated Liu Bei with great courtesy, but when advisers urged him to kill Liu Bei, Cao Cao refused for political reasons: killing a famous man who had come to him would damage his reputation and discourage other talents from joining him.

**Evidence from Sanguozhi and Pei Songzhi’s notes:**

1. **Cao Cao honored Liu Bei highly.**  
   In the *Sanguozhi*, *Shu Shu*, *Xianzhu Zhuan*: after Liu Bei came to Cao Cao, Cao Cao “treated him generously” (*hou yu zhi*) and made him *Yuzhou mu*. Later, after Lü Bu was destroyed, Liu Bei returned to Xu with Cao Cao. Cao Cao memorialized him as *zuo jiangjun* (Left General) and “treated him with even greater courtesy: when going out they shared the same carriage; when sitting they shared the same mat” (*chu ze tong yu, zuo ze tong xi*).  
   This shows Cao Cao regarded Liu Bei as a very important figure, not a mere defeated guest.

2. **Cao Cao explicitly called Liu Bei a true hero.**  
   In the *Xianzhu Zhuan*, Cao Cao once said calmly to Liu Bei:  
   “Today, the heroes under heaven are only you, Lord, and me. Men like Yuan Benchu are not worth counting.”  
   (*“今天下英雄，唯使君与操耳。本初之徒，不足数也。”*)  
   Liu Bei was eating and dropped his chopsticks.  
   Pei Songzhi’s note quoting the *Huayang Guozhi* adds that there happened to be thunder, and Liu Bei used it as an excuse. This is the famous “cooking wine and discussing heroes” scene later dramatized in *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*.  
   This is the clearest evidence that Cao Cao viewed Liu Bei as a peer-level rival, not a subordinate.

3. **Advisers urged Cao Cao to kill Liu Bei, but he refused.**  
   In the *Cheng Yu Zhuan*, Cheng Yu advised Cao Cao to kill Liu Bei. Cao Cao refused, saying in effect: “Now is the time to gather heroes. To kill one man and lose the hearts of the world—this cannot be done.”  
   Pei Songzhi’s note in the *Guo Jia Zhuan*, quoting the *Fu Zi*, says someone advised Cao Cao to deal with Liu Bei early because Liu Bei had heroic ambition. Cao Cao asked Guo Jia. Guo Jia argued that killing a famous man who had come in distress would make Cao Cao appear to harm the worthy; wise men would then doubt him and choose other lords. Cao Cao agreed.  
   So Cao Cao recognized Liu Bei as dangerous, but chose political reputation over immediate assassination.

**Romance vs. history:**  
In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, the “cooking wine” scene is expanded dramatically: Liu Bei hides by growing vegetables, Cao Cao invites him, delivers the hero line, and Liu Bei drops his chopsticks and uses thunder as a cover. Historically, the hero line and the dropped chopsticks are in Chen Shou’s main text; the thunder excuse appears in Pei Songzhi’s note quoting the *Huayang Guozhi*. The core idea—Cao Cao saw Liu Bei as a true hero and future threat—is historical, while the dramatic details are later elaboration.

q: In which year did Sima Yi remove Cao Shuang from power and take control of the government?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In **249 CE**. Sima Yi (Sima Yi) removed Cao Shuang (Cao Shuang) from power in the **first month of Zhengshi 10 / Jiaping 1**, i.e. **249**, in the coup known as the **Gaopingling incident**.

**Evidence from _Sanguozhi_ and Pei Songzhi’s notes:**  
In the _Sanguozhi_, _Wei shu_, “Cao Shuang zhuan,” the main text says:

> “In the tenth year, in the first month, the imperial carriage went to Gaopingling, and Cao Shuang and his brothers all accompanied it. Sima Xuanwang [Sima Yi] mobilized troops, first occupied the arsenal, and camped at the floating bridge over the Luo River.”

Sima Yi then memorialized to dismiss Cao Shuang and his associates from office. Cao Shuang hesitated and surrendered; afterward Cao Shuang and his faction were arrested, executed, and their clans wiped out. The _Qi Wang Fang ji_ places the event under **“Jiaping 1, spring, first month, jiawu day”**—also **249 CE**—and records Sima Yi’s memorial to dismiss Cao Shuang.

Pei Songzhi’s annotations add details such as Sima Yi feigning illness and Huan Fan’s advice to Cao Shuang, but they do not change the year. Thus, **249** is the year Sima Yi eliminated Cao Shuang’s power and took control of the Wei government.

q: Who came up with the idea of weighing an elephant by putting it on a boat and marking the waterline?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The idea is attributed to **Cao Chong**, a young son of **Cao Cao**. In Chinese this famous episode is called “Cao Chong weighs the elephant.”

**Evidence:** Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi*, in the *Wei Shu* biography of Deng’ai Wang Chong, records:

> At that time **Sun Quan** sent a giant elephant. **Taizu** [Cao Cao] wanted to know its weight. He asked his subordinates, but none could come up with a method. **Cao Chong** said: “Place the elephant on a large boat and mark the waterline. Then load other things onto the boat until the waterline is the same, and weigh those things; then you can compare and know.” Cao Cao was greatly pleased and had it carried out.

So this is not only a *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* invention; the official history also attributes the boat-and-waterline method to **Cao Chong**. I do not recall Pei Songzhi’s commentary giving a different inventor for this episode.

q: Who was Boyan? What was his original name?
reply:
Boyan (伯言) was the courtesy name (*zi*) of **Lu Xun** (陆逊), a leading Eastern Wu general and statesman, famous for defeating Liu Bei at Yiling/Xiaoting.

His original given name was **Lu Yi** (陆议). In other words: **Lu Xun, courtesy name Boyan, was originally named Lu Yi.**

Source: *Sanguozhi*, Wu Shu, “Lu Xun zhuan”: “陆逊字伯言，吴郡吴人也。本名议……” — “Lu Xun, courtesy name Boyan, a man of Wu County in Wu Commandery. His original name was Yi…”

q: Who was the Marquis Shunping (Marquis Who Was Obedient and Peaceful)?
reply:
**Conclusion:** “Marquis Shunping” (Shunping Hou 顺平侯) was **Zhao Yun** (赵云, Zhao Yun; courtesy name **Zilong** 子龙), the famous Shu Han general. “Shunping” was his **posthumous noble title**, not a normal place-name marquisate. The English rendering “Marquis Who Was Obedient and Peaceful” is approximate; the title is better explained by the posthumous-name rules cited in the sources.

**Evidence from the histories:**

- Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi*, *Shu shu*, “Zhao Yun zhuan” says:  
  “赵云字子龙，常山真定人也。……七年卒，追谥顺平侯。”  
  That is, Zhao Yun died in the seventh year of Jianxing (229 CE), and was posthumously titled **Shunping Hou**.

- Pei Songzhi’s commentary quotes the *Yun Biezhuan* 云别传, recording the court discussion under Liu Shan:  
  “谨按谥法，柔贤慈惠曰顺，执事有班曰平，克定祸乱曰平，应谥云曰顺平侯。”  
  So “Shun” and “Ping” are posthumous epithets, and the full title is **Zhao Yun, Marquis Shunping**.

- The *Sanguozhi*, “Houzhu zhuan” dates the posthumous grant to **Jingyao 4** (261 CE), when Liu Shan posthumously titled Zhao Yun.

**Romance note:** In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, Zhao Yun is famous as one of the “Five Tiger Generals” (五虎大将). Historically, the “Five Tiger Generals” was not an official Shu Han institution, though Chen Shou did group Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, Ma Chao, Huang Zhong, and Zhao Yun in one biographical section. The title **Shunping Hou** itself, however, is historical.

q: How many sons did Cao Cao have in total?
reply:
According to Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi*, Cao Cao had **25 recorded sons**.

Evidence: In *Wei shu*, volume 20, *Wuwen shiwang gong zhuan* (“Biographies of the Princes and Dukes of Emperor Wu and Emperor Wen”), Chen Shou explicitly begins: **“武皇帝二十五男”** — “Emperor Wu had twenty-five sons.” He then lists them by their mothers, including Cao Pi, Cao Zhang, Cao Zhi, Cao Xiong, Cao Ang, Cao Shuo, Cao Chong, Cao Biao, and others.

Pei Songzhi’s commentary adds details about their lives and fates, but it does not change this total. This count refers to Cao Cao’s biological sons as recorded in the *Sanguozhi*; adopted or nephew-like figures such as Cao Zhen are not counted in this list, and daughters are separate.

q: Who was called the 'Tiger Fool' (Huchi), and how did he get that nickname?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The man called “Tiger Fool” (*Huchi* 虎痴) was **Xu Chu** (许褚), courtesy name **Zhongkang** (仲康), a famous Wei general under **Cao Cao**.

**How he got the nickname:** According to his biography in the *San Guo Zhi* (Wei Shu, Xu Chu zhuan), the soldiers in the army gave him the name because he had tiger-like strength but was simple-minded / blunt / “foolish” in temperament. The text says:

> “军中以褚力如虎而痴，故号曰虎痴。”  
> “In the army, because Chu’s strength was like a tiger and he was *chi* [foolish/simple], they nicknamed him *Huchi* [Tiger Fool].”

The same passage also records the famous Tong Pass episode: **Ma Chao** asked Cao Cao, “Where is your ‘Tiger Marquis’ (*Hu Hou* 虎侯)?” Cao Cao pointed to Xu Chu. Xu Chu glared at Ma Chao, and Ma Chao did not dare make a move. The text adds that from this, the world called him by that name.

**Romance vs. history:** In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, Xu Chu is also called *Huchi*, and the Tong Pass confrontation with Ma Chao is dramatized. But the core nickname and its explanation—tiger-like strength plus a simple/foolish nature—come from the official *San Guo Zhi* record.

q: Whose daughter was Diaochan, and how did she drive a wedge between Dong Zhuo and Lü Bu?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In the official *Sanguozhi* (Chen Shou’s text and Pei Songzhi’s commentary), **Diaochan does not exist**. She is a fictional character from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*. In the novel, she is **Wang Yun’s adopted daughter**—more precisely, a singing girl in his household whom he treated as his daughter, not his biological daughter. She was used by Wang Yun to sow suspicion between **Dong Zhuo** and **Lü Bu**.

**In the Romance version:**  
Wang Yun first promised Diaochan to Lü Bu, then gave her to Dong Zhuo. Diaochan then played both sides: she told Lü Bu that Dong Zhuo had taken her by force, and she told Dong Zhuo that Lü Bu was harassing her. The climax is the “Fengyi Pavilion” scene, where Dong Zhuo catches Lü Bu with Diaochan and throws a halberd at him. This deepens the rift. Wang Yun then persuades Lü Bu to join the plot, and Lü Bu eventually kills Dong Zhuo.

**In official history:**  
There is no Diaochan and no such daughter of Wang Yun. *Sanguozhi·Lü Bu Zhuan* says Lü Bu guarded Dong Zhuo’s inner apartments and had an illicit affair with one of Dong Zhuo’s maidservants; he feared discovery. Dong Zhuo once angrily threw a hand-halberd at Lü Bu, and Lü Bu dodged it. Later, Wang Yun persuaded Lü Bu to turn against Dong Zhuo. The maidservant is unnamed, and the histories do not say she was Wang Yun’s daughter or that she deliberately drove a wedge between them. That is the Romance invention.

q: Sun Quan urged one of his generals to study more; later Lu Su was amazed at how much he had learned. Who was this general, and what did he reply to Lu Su?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The general was **Lü Meng** (吕蒙, pinyin: **Lü Meng**; courtesy name **Ziming** 子明). His famous reply to Lu Su was:

> **“士别三日，即更刮目相待。”**  
> “After three days apart, one should look at a man with new eyes.”

In the more familiar *Zizhi Tongjian* version, this is often quoted with the continuation: **“大兄何见事之晚乎！”** (“Elder brother, why have you realized this so late!”).

**Evidence from the *Sanguozhi* tradition:**

- In Chen Shou’s main text of the *Sanguozhi* (*Wu Shu*, Lu Meng’s biography), Lu Su succeeded Zhou Yu and passed by Lü Meng’s camp. Lu Su still somewhat looked down on Lü Meng. Lü Meng asked how Lu Su planned to guard against Guan Yu; Lu Su casually said “improvise as needed.” Lü Meng then outlined five strategies. Lu Su was amazed, left his seat, patted Lü Meng’s back, and said:  
  **“吕子明，吾不知卿才略所及乃至于此也。”**  
  “Lü Ziming, I did not know your talent and strategic ability reached this level.”

- Pei Songzhi’s annotation quotes the *Jiang Biao Zhuan* for the study episode: Sun Quan urged **Lü Meng and Jiang Qin** to study. Lü Meng began studying diligently. Later Lu Su, after discussing with him, said:  
  **“吾谓弟但有武略耳，至于今者，学识英博，非复吴下阿蒙。”**  
  “I thought you had only military skill; now your learning is broad and erudite—you are no longer the Ameng of Wu.”  
  Lü Meng replied:  
  **“士别三日，即更刮目相待。”**

So this is not merely a *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* invention; its core appears in Pei Songzhi’s note to the *Sanguozhi*, though the popular textbook passage “孙权劝学” is from the *Zizhi Tongjian*.
